Rotala macrandra is native to India, particularly four isolated localities in the South Indian states of Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu. It thrives in marshy soils and grows in streams, flooded paddy fields, riverbanks and temporary ponds. It grows both emersed and submersed, and its growth form varies significantly with light and nutrient availability.
This plant needs a large space because of its growth potential. The recommended tank size is a minimum of 10 gallons (about 40 litres).

This stem plant is not beginner-friendly. It needs high-intensity lighting, stable CO2 injection and lean water-column fertilization to grow optimally and remain vibrant. When macronutrients are insufficient, the lower leaves deteriorate; a lack of micronutrients causes poor colouring and other problems. Once settled, it grows fairly fast.

Prune overgrown stems regularly with sharp scissors so they do not reach the surface, and replant the tops or discard them. Change about 25% of the water weekly with dechlorinated water to maintain water quality and remove excess nitrate. Keep to a regular, lean fertilization regime providing the macro- and micronutrients needed.
Cut the longest stems 5-10 cm from the ground and replant them in the group.

• Temperature: 22–26 °C.
  • pH: 6.0–7.5; the plant prefers acidic water.
  • Hardness: soft water is required, with 3–8 dKH.
  • CO2: injection is required; recommended level 15–25 ppm. The plant does not tolerate CO2 fluctuations, which may stunt the tips, especially in less hardy varieties.
  • For deep red colouring: phosphate about 1.5–2.0 ppm and nitrate below 10 ppm.

If you keep shrimp with this plant, note that high CO2 and copper (present in most fertilizers) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Lighting: Rotala macrandra is demanding. Most varieties need high-intensity lighting to thrive and keep intense colouring; use quality LED aquarium lighting or another good light source, and maintain suitable PAR and a standard photoperiod. The lower parts of the plant may melt due to inadequate light or shading by taller plants.

Substrate: the plant needs a nutrient-rich substrate. Enriched aqua soils hold ammonia and essential nutrients and help develop thicker stems and healthy, fleshy foliage. Recommended substrates:

  • ADA Amazonia aqua soil
  • Carib Sea Eco-Complete
  • Seachem Fluorite

Rotala macrandra is a colourful stem plant of the family Lythraceae, commonly called Giant Red Rotala for its deep red colouring. It has soft, delicate leaves growing oppositely on thick, vertical stems, which can reach 20–30 cm about six weeks after planting. Leaves are mainly red, but may be green, pink, tan or orange depending on variety or cultivar; they are mostly ovoid or obovate, and somewhat tapering or lanceolate in some varieties. Grown emersed, the plant is denser and the leaves broader and mostly green. Under optimal conditions, tiny oxygen bubbles form on the leaf tips ("pearling").

Varieties

  • 'Variegated': magenta-red or pink with tan and orange tinges, large wavy leaves and white venation; more difficult to grow.
  • Green varieties: tall stems, mostly green foliage with little pink or red towards the top; the easiest varieties.
  • Red varieties: red foliage from top to bottom; generally more difficult to grow.
  • 'Narrow leaf': profusely branching, with many narrow, near-lanceolate, bright red leaves.
  • 'Mini butterfly': resembles Rotala rotundifolia but with a deeper red tone and slightly outward-rolled leaf edges; hard to grow, especially in low-tech tanks.
  • 'Mini type 4 green': moderately sized soft green leaves with serrated edges; develops orange hues under high light.
  • 'Mini type 4 red': like type 4 green but deep red overall; needs high light, nutrient-rich substrate and adequate water-column fertilization.
  • 'Mini type 2': leaves with curled edges, mostly green with pink and orange hues; difficult to maintain long term.

Planting and propagation

Ideal for the midground and background. It can create strong focal points in Nature and Japanese style aquascapes, or be set in streets/layers in Dutch style aquascapes.

  • Untie the bunch and divide it into several portions.
  • Disinfect the plantlets (if not grown in vitro).
  • Place the individual stems in the enriched substrate, spaced about 5–8 cm apart to prevent overcrowding and shading.
  • Dose liquid fertilizers at the start and as the plants grow.

Propagation is by cuttings: cut the tops, about 10–15 cm of the stems, and replant them in the substrate. Keep proper spacing, fertilize and trim regularly to encourage multiple side shoots. The dry start method is another way to grow it; it provides unlimited CO2, but the transition to water can make the plant melt.

Problems

  • Stunted, curling tips: usually caused by unstable or inconsistent CO2 or over-fertilization. Leaf edges and tips crumble, curl and/or wither. Solution: check CO2 and fertilization.
  • Chlorosis (pale leaves): mostly caused by iron deficiency. Solution: raise the level of chelated iron in the water column.
  • Turning brown: the plant is sensitive to sterilizing agents; the more tender the tissue, the greater the damage.
  • Melting: a finicky plant that needs stable water parameters; sudden changes can make it melt.
  • Leggy bottom leaves (bare stems at the base): when the plant becomes very dense, the bottom leaves die back from lack of light. Solution: give more space and trim regularly.

Benefits

  • Aquascape: its shape and form make an excellent decorative addition.
  • Easy to move: it has a weak root system and can be moved or removed easily without pulling up substrate.
  • Hiding place: cover and shade for invertebrates, shrimp and small fish.
  • Foraging: provides biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Oxygenation: oxygenates and aerates the water.

Compatible tankmates

  • Fish: bettas, tetras, pearl gourami, honey gourami, zebra danio, cherry barbs, platies, guppies, endlers, mollies, otocinclus, pygmy corydoras, etc.
  • Snails: Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails, etc.
  • Dwarf shrimp: all Neocaridina (Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Snowball, Black Rose, Orange Sakura, Green Jade, Rili, etc.) or Caridina (Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti, Blue Tiger, etc.), Amano shrimp, ghost shrimp, bamboo shrimp, vampire shrimp, etc.

Avoid species that may damage the plant or eat it, such as koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. Do not keep it with most crayfish or freshwater crabs, which cut, eat and uproot plants.

The plant is readily available in fish stores and nurseries worldwide. A bunch may contain up to 7 fresh, healthy stems. Choose healthy, lush specimens free of cuts, tears or discoloration.

Rotala macrandra is more suitable for experienced aquarists because of the high demands and special care required to keep it healthy and well coloured.

Rotala macrandra 'Japan' is a magnificent aquarium plant, but unfortunately, it is very demanding. This variant is a little easier to grow and develops better coloration. It needs very good light to develop its beautiful red shades, just like CO2 addition and soft water are vital to ensure optimal growth.
